name: Priya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the floor lead at Ashby Hosiery, a family-owned sock factory, third generation, Mr Ashby's grandfather started it. I look after a room of forty circular knitting machines, they look like big metal drums that spin and knit a sock tube in about two minutes. My day is fixing dropped stitches, swapping yarn cones, changing needles when one breaks, and keeping the two apprentices from getting their sleeves caught. I can tell by the sound which machine has a bent needle before the sock even comes out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a two-year technical diploma in textiles and started at Ashby on an apprenticeship. The woman who trained me, Mrs Kowal, had been there since she was sixteen. I married Daniel last year, he works at the builders' merchant, and we're renting while we save, about four months put by. I use AI sometimes, my cousin set it up on my phone, mostly to look up fault codes on the newer machines when the manual's useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Honestly, that's what I'd half expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get back to work. We've got orders to fill. I'd probably say that to the girls on the floor and to Daniel, and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. Our machines already do most of the knitting. What they need is someone who understands them, and that's me. If AI stays a thing for looking up fault codes, nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are. Daniel and I would keep saving for a house and probably start trying for a baby in a year or two. At work I'd keep training the apprentices properly, like Mrs Kowal did with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like a good week where the orders come in and nobody's sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does training the apprentices matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how this trade works. Somebody gave me their time when I was nineteen and knew nothing. If I don't pass it on, the knowledge just walks out the door when I do. Mr Ashby says the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more if it stayed like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, maybe, once I saw it was reliable. It saved me a whole morning last month on a fault code. But I wouldn't let the apprentices use it instead of learning the machine properly.

S0.say: She'd say it's time to get back to work and fill orders. She'd say it to the women on the floor and her husband and leave it there.
S0.think: She'd be relieved, believing the machines need someone who understands them and that she is that person. If AI stays a fault-code tool, nothing changes.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, saving for a house with her husband and planning to try for a baby in a year or two. Keeps training apprentices the way she was trained.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like a good week with steady orders.
S0.quote: If I don't pass it on, the knowledge just walks out the door when I do.
S0.fieldNote: Priya values passing on skills through apprenticeship as a duty. She uses AI cautiously and would not let it replace proper learning. Family plans are front and centre for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That sounds more like the real thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation has had to learn new things, and people who work hard will manage. The Ashby family has kept us going through hard times before. I'd trust them to do right by us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried about the room. If the machines start fixing their own needles and changing their own yarn, they'll need fewer of us on the floor. I'd probably stay, but some of the others wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw it working at Ashby, I'd learn the new systems properly, and use the AI tools more for faults and planning. I'd keep saving and probably wait a bit longer before trying for a baby, maybe another year. I'd keep training the apprentices, but on the new kit as well as the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust the Ashby family. What would they have to do to lose that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bring in robots and let people go without a word. Mr Ashby isn't like that. But his son is coming into the business, and he's all spreadsheets. I don't know him as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on the floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea, she's fifty-nine, been here forty years. She's quick with her hands but she hates screens. I'd want her to be able to finish out her time with dignity.

S1.say: She'd say every generation has had to learn new things and hard workers will manage. She'd trust the owning family to do right by staff, as they have in hard times before.
S1.think: She'd worry that self-maintaining machines would mean fewer people on the floor. She'd probably stay but expects some colleagues wouldn't.
S1.do: Learns the new systems and uses AI tools more once she sees them working at her factory. Keeps saving and delays trying for a baby by about a year, and trains apprentices on both old and new equipment.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful but not panicking.
S1.quote: But his son is coming into the business, and he's all spreadsheets.
S1.fieldNote: Priya trusts the factory's owners rather than government or unions, but her trust is personal and may not pass to the next generation. She adapts once change is proven locally. She worries about older colleagues finishing their careers with dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's frightening. We haven't even got a house yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to pull together, because the government won't be quick enough. And I'd say the companies that make this stuff should answer for it. I'd say that at work and at my mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think the floor would be empty within a year of it arriving. Our machines already knit by themselves. Add a robot that can change needles and fix dropped stitches, and they don't need anyone. Four months of savings isn't much against that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the house and turn that into an emergency fund straight away, and we'd put off a baby. I'd cut everything we don't need. If the job went, we'd lean on Daniel's job and family, his parents have room, and I'd look for anything hands-on locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's a lot of lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, the baby has to wait. And he'd go quiet, because he wants one more than I do, if anything. Then he'd say, 'we'll manage', which is what he always says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest one. They're eighteen and nineteen. I'd tell them to finish their certificates anyway, because something on paper is better than nothing. But I wouldn't really believe it.

S2.say: She'd say families and communities must pull together because government won't act fast enough, and that AI companies should answer for it.
S2.think: She thinks the knitting floor would empty within a year once robots could do needle changes and repairs. Her four months of savings feel small against that.
S2.do: Turns house savings into an emergency fund at once and postpones having a baby. Cuts non-essentials, and if the job went would rely on her husband's income and his parents while looking for local hands-on work.
S2.quote: I'd tell them to finish their certificates anyway, because something on paper is better than nothing. But I wouldn't really believe it.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast version Priya's plans to start a family are the first casualty. She turns to family rather than the state and blames the companies building the technology. Her honesty about not believing her own advice to apprentices stands out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to learn something new if you start now. I'd say it to the apprentices especially. Don't wait for someone to tell you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is enough for me to retrain in something people want a person for. I've always thought I'd be good at caring for people, my gran's carers were wonderful. That's the kind of work I'd look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a healthcare assistant course in evenings and weekends in the second year, once I'd seen that people actually got jobs from it. I'd keep saving towards six months. We'd probably have a baby around year three, before it all arrives, rather than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have the baby before it arrives rather than waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if we wait for it to be safe, we might never do it. Daniel and I talked about this kind of thing once, when the factory down the road shut. We said we'd rather be a family going through it together than two people waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work rather than staying in textiles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't think a robot changing needles is far off, but I think people will still want a person holding their hand when they're old. Maybe I'm wrong. But that's my best guess.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to learn something new if people start now, especially urging the apprentices not to wait.
S3.think: She believes five years is enough to retrain into work where people want a human, such as caring, inspired by her grandmother's carers.
S3.do: Starts an evening and weekend healthcare assistant course in year two once she sees it leads to jobs. Keeps saving towards six months and plans to have a baby around year three rather than waiting.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadied by taking action.
S3.quote: We said we'd rather be a family going through it together than two people waiting.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Priya plans to move into care work and decides not to postpone a family indefinitely. She retrains only after seeing proof it works. Her reasoning rests on a belief that people will still want human care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a lot more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to plan for, if people are sensible. Learn a trade, look after your family, don't expect someone else to sort it out for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel fairly okay. I'd stay at Ashby for a good few years, have our children, then retrain when it started to bite. I'd keep teaching the apprentices, because they'll need a trade even in that world, if only for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ashby for the next few years and keep saving. We'd start trying for a baby within a year or two as we planned. Around year four or five, I'd start the healthcare assistant course and maybe go on to nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd feel all right about my own plans, but the end of it still bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bothers you about the end of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my children would grow up in a world where nobody needs them to work. I was raised to think work makes you who you are. I don't know what I'd teach them instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change how you see the Ashby family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I think they'd do their best. But in ten years it'll be the son running it. I'd hope he remembers who knitted for his grandfather.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty to plan for, urging people to learn a trade and look after their families rather than expecting others to sort it out.
S4.think: She'd feel fairly okay, planning to stay at her factory for some years, have children and retrain later. She'd keep teaching apprentices because they need a trade, at least for a while.
S4.do: Keeps going at the factory and saving for several years. Starts trying for a baby within a year or two, and around year four or five begins a healthcare assistant course, possibly moving on to nursing.
S4.feel: Uneasy: confident in her own plans but troubled by the end point.
S4.quote: I was raised to think work makes you who you are. I don't know what I'd teach them instead.
S4.fieldNote: For Priya the decade lets her keep family plans and retrain later. Her deeper worry is moral: what to teach children in a world without work. Her trust in the owning family is tempered by doubts about the next generation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We'd have no house, no baby and no job, all at once. What would help is apprenticeships for grown-ups, in things that will still need people, that you can do while still earning. And employers giving honest notice, like the old families used to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apprentices. They're the ones who've just started and been told this is a trade for life. I said the same thing to them that Mrs Kowal said to me. I'm not sure I can say it now.

headlineQuote: I can tell by the sound which machine has a bent needle before the sock even comes out.
portrait: Priya Torres is twenty-seven, the floor lead in a room of forty knitting machines at a family-owned sock factory, married last year to Daniel, who works at a builders' merchant. They rent, have about four months saved and hope to buy a house and start a family. She trusts the owning family, values apprenticeships and uses AI cautiously once she sees it works. She is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, but alarmed by AGI in two years, which would push back the baby and the house. With five or ten years she plans a move into care work and decides not to put off children, worrying most about what to teach them about work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because they would lose the chance of a house, a baby and her job all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Adult apprenticeships in work that will still need people, done while earning, and honest notice from employers.
